summary: Describes a DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 option and an IPv6 Router Advertisement option that tell a client the address of a captive portal API. Captive portals, as at coffee shops, restrict what users can do until they satisfy some conditions. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: When you join public Wi-Fi, the network can quietly hand your device the address of its welcome page. This document defines how, so your device knows where to go to get online.

questions: how do devices discover a captive portal
what is the captive portal dhcp option
what is the captive portal ipv6 ra option
subtitle: How a network hands a device the address of its captive portal API through DHCP and IPv6 Router Advertisements.

tldr.problem: Captive portals restrict users until they accept terms or pay, and today they have to intercept connections in ways that resemble man-in-the-middle attacks, which will work less well as end nodes get more security-minded.
tldr.mechanism: A DHCPv4 option (code 114), a DHCPv6 option (code 103) and an IPv6 Router Advertisement option (type 37) each carry the URI of the captive portal API endpoint.
tldr.outcome: Clients learn directly that they are behind a captive portal and where to contact it. RFC 8910 obsoletes RFC 7710 and moves the DHCPv4 code from 160 to 114.

facts.label: Max URI length in IPv4 DHCP

today: RFC 8910 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7710 and updates RFC 3679. It has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Problem With Captive Portals
sections.content:
In places such as coffee shops, users often must connect to a captive portal device and agree to an Acceptable Use Policy or give billing information before they get Internet access. To show those pages, the enforcement device has to intercept the user's connections and redirect them, using methods very similar to man-in-the-middle attacks. The RFC notes that as end nodes become more security-conscious, these tricks will become less effective or more intrusive.

This document does not define how the portal works. It only lets the client know that it is behind a portal and how to contact it, using DHCPv4, DHCPv6 and IPv6 Router Advertisement options. The specific methods of satisfying and interacting with the portal are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Some Wi-Fi makes you click a welcome page before you can use it, and it does this by sneakily steering you there. This document lets the network simply tell your device where the page is.

sections.title: The Captive-Portal Option
sections.content:
The option tells the client it may be behind a captive portal and provides the URI of an API defined by RFC 8908. The goal is mainly to show the user the portal information faster and more reliably. The RFC adds that portals will still need interception for legacy clients and clients will still need to probe, but this mechanism is the preferred way to detect a captive portal.

Clients that support the DHCP option SHOULD include it in the Parameter Request List in DHCPREQUEST messages, and servers MAY send it without being asked. A network can provision the same URI by several methods (IPv4 DHCP, IPv6 DHCP and IPv6 RA) to cover different classes of client, and the operator SHOULD make the URIs identical.

The URI SHOULD NOT contain an IP address literal. A network with no captive portal can say so by using the URI urn:ietf:params:capport:unrestricted, and clients seeing it may skip time-consuming forms of portal detection.
sections.eli5: The network tells your device, here is the address of the welcome page. If there is no welcome page, it says so with a special no-restrictions address, and your device can stop checking.

sections.title: The Three Option Formats
sections.content:
All three options carry one URI, encoded following the rules of RFC 3986, and none of them is null terminated.

  • DHCPv4: a one-octet code (114), a one-octet length in octets, then the URI.
  • DHCPv6: a two-octet option-code (103), a 16-bit option-len in octets, then the URI.
  • IPv6 RA: a Type of 37, an 8-bit Length counted in units of 8 bytes (including the Type and Length fields), then the URI, which MUST be padded with NUL (0x00) so the total option length is a multiple of 8 bytes.

The maximum URI length that fits in IPv4 DHCP is 255 bytes, so URIs longer than that SHOULD NOT be provisioned by any of the IPv6 options. In IPv6-only environments this restriction can be relaxed.
sections.eli5: Each version is a small envelope with a label saying what it is, how long the address is, and the address itself. The RA version gets padded with blanks so it fits neat 8-byte slots.

sections.title: Content Negotiation and Precedence
sections.content:
A portal MAY do content negotiation and try to redirect clients that do not explicitly list application/capport+json in an Accept header. It then SHOULD redirect them to the value of the user-portal-url API key. Because such responses might be cached, implementors SHOULD include a suitable Vary header or set Cache-Control to private or something stricter such as no-store.

A device may learn portal URIs from more than one option. Implementations may choose their own order of precedence. If the URIs learned are not all identical, the condition should be logged for the owner or administrator, and it is a network configuration error.
sections.eli5: If your device hears the welcome page address from two places and they disagree, it may pick either one, but it should write down that the network is set up wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Removing or reducing the need for interception makes the portal and its actions visible instead of hidden, and makes it less likely users switch off safeguards such as DNSSEC validation or VPNs to reach the portal. Because the system knows it is behind a portal, it can avoid sending cookies and credentials. Clients SHOULD validate that the option contents conform to the requirements for URIs.

These options travel over the same protocols as other critical configuration, so the same weaknesses apply. Without measures such as RA-Guard or DHCPv6-Shield, an attacker could inject, modify or block DHCP messages or RAs, and use these options to send users to an address of the attacker's choosing. The RFC says an attacker able to do this could already list itself as the default gateway, but that this document removes the need for interception and so may make the attack easier.

Since the operating system or application knows it is contacting a portal, it can render the page in a sandbox and label it untrusted. The RFC leaves those details to implementors. It also notes that automatically connecting devices could be tracked using these techniques, but that this is already possible with current portal mechanisms.
sections.eli5: A trickster who can fake the network's message could send you to a fake welcome page. Because your device knows it is a welcome page, it can be extra careful with it.

sections.title: Registrations and the Code Change
sections.content:
IANA registered a new URN, capport:unrestricted, in the IETF URN sub-namespace for registered protocol parameter identifiers. It also set DHCPv4 option tag 114 to "DHCP Captive-Portal" and updated the existing DHCPv6 (103) and IPv6 ND (37) registrations to reference this document.

The earlier RFC 7710 used DHCPv4 code 160. During an experiment at IETF 106 in Singapore, some Polycom devices on the same network were found to use option 160 for other purposes, and seeing a captive portal URL there caused them not to work as desired. IANA therefore deprecated code 160 and allocated 114, which is also why this document updates RFC 3679.
sections.eli5: The old DHCP number was already being used by some phones for something else and they got confused. So the number was changed to a new, unused one.

items.label: DHCPv4 Code
items.desc: One octet; replaces code 160 from RFC 7710.

items.label: DHCPv6 option-code
items.desc: Two octets; the length is a 16-bit count of URI octets.

items.label: IPv6 RA Type
items.desc: Length is in units of 8 bytes; the URI is NUL padded.
